samples.summary: Attacker-triggerable timeout message steers the user to `--allow-unbound-callback`, re-creating the downgrade lever the design claims to have closed
samples.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` (login.ts:309) is set by ANY `GET /callback?code=…` with no `state` — a request every local process and every visited page can make (only the ephemeral port is needed; a local process reads it from `ss -ltn`, a page can scan). At login.ts:376-382 that flag replaces the neutral 'Login timed out' with `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE`, whose text (login.ts:222-226) tells the user to 'Upgrade the server, or re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback`'. Full chain: (1) attacker consumes the one-time `/start` via a `no-cors` fetch (login.ts:266-281), so the browser tab launched by `open()` gets a 410 and no real callback ever arrives; (2) attacker sends one nonce-less `/callback?code=x` to set the flag; (3) at 30s the CLI reports the version-skew message and points the user at the opt-out; (4) the user re-runs with `--allow-unbound-callback`, at which point login.ts:306 no longer rejects a nonce-less callback and the attacker's `?code=<attacker code>` is accepted, exchanged, and saved as the machine's session (an account-injection: the victim's subsequent CLI writes go into the attacker's workspace). The comment at login.ts:298-305 explicitly names this hazard ('steer the user at the flag that turns the binding off would hand an attacker a downgrade lever') but only suppresses it in the immediate `warn()`, not in the timeout error. The message should be gated on evidence the callback was genuine (e.g. only shown when nothing at all arrived, or never machine-suggested), not on an attacker-settable flag.

samples.summary: Loopback listener performs no Host/Origin validation, so the new nonce-disclosing `GET /start` is reachable via DNS rebinding
samples.evidence: The request handler parses only `req.url` against a hard-coded base (`new URL(req.url ?? '/', 'http://127.0.0.1')`, login.ts:262) and never inspects `req.headers.host`, `Origin`, or `Sec-Fetch-Site`. `/start` (login.ts:266-281) then returns a 302 whose `Location` is the authorize URL containing the `cliState` nonce, to any requester. The design doc (docs/design/cli.md, 'the same-origin policy keeps it from reading the `Location` of a `no-cors` fetch') assumes a visited page is cross-origin to the listener — DNS rebinding defeats that: a page served from `http://evil.example:<guessed-port>` that rebinds `evil.example` to 127.0.0.1 is SAME-ORIGIN with the listener, so `fetch('/start', {redirect:'manual'})` returns a readable response and discloses the nonce. With the nonce the attacker starts their own OAuth flow at `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim port>&cliState=<stolen nonce>`, and the backend (auth.controller.ts:133) redirects an authorization code for the ATTACKER's GitHub account to the victim's listener with a matching `state`, which login.ts:322 then accepts — the victim's CLI is silently logged into the attacker's account. Preconditions are port guessing inside the 30s window plus rebinding, so this is not trivial, but the fix is one line: reject any request whose `Host` is not `127.0.0.1:<port>`/`localhost:<port>`, and reject requests carrying an `Origin` header. Note this listener had no Host check before either, but this change is what put a secret behind it.

samples.summary: The `cliState` nonce is transmitted as a URL query parameter, so it lands in backend/proxy access logs and browser history
samples.evidence: `buildAuthorizeUrl` puts the nonce in `GET ${server}/auth/github?...&cliState=<nonce>` (login.ts:209-212), which the backend reads from `req.query.cliState` (github-auth.guard.ts:65). Query strings are recorded by default in Nest/Express access logs, reverse proxies, CDNs and WAFs, and in the browser's history/session-restore data. Anyone able to read those logs during the 5-minute state TTL learns the nonce for a specific `port`, and can then complete an OAuth flow that redirects an attacker-owned authorization code to `127.0.0.1:<port>/callback` with the matching `state` — the loopback check at login.ts:322 passes. This materially weakens the binding the change is built around; the same secret sent as a header or via the PKCE-shaped `POST /auth/cli/start` sketched in the comments would not be logged. Worth at minimum documenting in the rest-api.md risk table alongside the argv/stderr entry, which currently implies the nonce is not written anywhere durable.

samples.summary: `normalizeCliState` is only reached inside the valid-port branch, so a malformed `cliState` with an out-of-range port is silently dropped and the request degrades to the cookie-setting web flow
samples.evidence: `normalizeCliState(cliState)` is called at github-auth.guard.ts:70, nested inside `if (Number.isInteger(portNum) && portNum >= 1024 && portNum <= 65535)` (line 69). A request such as `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=80&cliState=<garbage>` therefore never validates `cliState`; no state token is injected, so `githubAuthCallback` receives no `state` query and falls through to the default web flow at auth.controller.ts:145-149, which mints and sets `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` cookies in the browser and redirects to `FRONTEND_URL`. That contradicts the contract stated in the guard's own doc comment ('A present-but-malformed nonce is a 400 ... never a silent drop') and in rest-api.md, and means a caller who thinks they are doing a CLI login can instead be silently issued a browser session. Validate `cliState` (and reject an invalid CLI `port`) before the port range check when `mode === 'cli'`.

samples.summary: `--allow-unbound-callback` disables the binding entirely rather than only for the legitimate skew case, so the trivially-forged nonce-less callback wins
samples.evidence: With `allowUnbound` set, login.ts:306 short-circuits and login.ts:322 only rejects a callback that carries a WRONG state — a callback carrying NO state is accepted outright. An injector therefore does not need to guess or steal the nonce; omitting `state` is sufficient (`GET /callback?code=<attacker code>`), and the code is exchanged at login.ts:86 and persisted as the machine's session at login.ts:168. The flag is documented as an escape hatch, but it is an all-or-nothing kill switch on the whole binding rather than, say, a first-wins-with-confirmation prompt, and finding #1 above shows an attacker can nudge a user into enabling it. At minimum the flag should require an interactive confirmation of the resulting account (`Logged in as X — is that you?`) before `saveSession`.

verdict.reason: The finding's evidence checks out line-for-line. `sawUnboundCallback` (login.ts:248) is set at login.ts:309-310 by ANY `GET /callback?code=x` with no `state` param — the only prerequisites are the ephemeral port and a non-empty `code` (login.ts:290); there is no origin, nonce, or authenticity check on that branch. At login.ts:373-385 that attacker-settable flag selects `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` over the neutral 'Login timed out' text, and that message (login.ts:222-226) explicitly instructs the user to 're-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback`'. The attacker can force the timeout path deterministically because `/start` is one-shot (login.ts:272-277 `startConsumed`): a racing local process or a cross-origin `no-cors` fetch consumes it, leaving the browser tab launched at login.ts:72 with a 410 so no genuine callback ever arrives. If the user follows the suggestion, login.ts:49 sets `allowUnbound`, login.ts:306 stops rejecting nonce-less callbacks, and an injected `?code=` falls through to `callbackResolve(code)` (login.ts:367-370), is exchanged (login.ts:86-90) and saved as the machine session (login.ts:168) — authorization-code/account injection. No guard elsewhere suppresses this: the comment at login.ts:298-305 names this exact hazard and the test at packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:104 asserts only that the immediate `warn()` omits the flag, confirming the mitigation was never extended to the timeout error. Not `not-present` (code is verbatim), not `already-guarded` (no such guard exists), not `out-of-scope` (this is an auth-binding downgrade lever, squarely authorization/auth-flow, and a major security weakness under this rubric).

verdict.reason: The absence is real: the loopback listener's only request handler (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:261-371, the sole createServer in packages/cli/src) derives everything from req.url against the hard-coded base at line 262 and never reads req.headers.host, Origin, or Sec-Fetch-Site. A repo-wide grep finds Host/Origin validation only in node_modules (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk .../hostHeaderValidation.js:22, hono csrf) and in the unrelated packages/design-editor/src/plugin/bridge.ts:111 — nothing reachable from login.ts, directly or via a helper. GET /start (login.ts:266-281) does hand out a 302 whose Location carries the cliState nonce built at login.ts:204-213, and the backend at packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:119-135 will echo an attacker-supplied cliState with an authorization code to an attacker-chosen loopback port, which login.ts:322 accepts on nonce match — so the account-takeover chain is real once the nonce leaks. Tests (packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts) cover 404/410/state-mismatch but no Host/Origin case, so this is unguarded, not guarded-and-untested. In lane (sensitive data exposure / auth bypass) and major: a secret-bearing route on a loopback listener with no Host check is the classic DNS-rebinding gap. Caveat on exploitability only: fetch with redirect:'manual' returns an opaque-redirect response with an empty header list even same-origin, so the specific read primitive named may not actually disclose Location; that lowers demonstrated exploitability but does not supply a counterexample to the missing control, so the finding stays on the gate.

finding.summary: `GET /start` hands the login nonce to any unauthenticated local client, widening the nonce-theft surface the change claims to close
finding.evidence:
The new route answers the *first* request on the loopback port with `302 Location: ` (login.ts:277-279) with no authentication, no caller identification and no rate limit. Attack: a local process polls `curl -s -D- http://127.0.0.1:

/start` across the ephemeral port range (the port is trivially discoverable — it is printed to stderr at login.ts:67 and is the same port that appears in the browser's authorize URL) and wins the race against `open()`, which needs hundreds of ms to spawn a browser. It now holds the 32-byte nonce, so it can (a) drive its own `GET ${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=&cliState=` — the backend accepts any well-formed nonce (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:70) and echoes it on the loopback redirect (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:130-135) — and (b) deliver `GET http://127.0.0.1:

/callback?code=&state=` to the victim's listener, which passes `stateMatches` (login.ts:322) and settles the login, so the victim's `session.json` is written with the *attacker's* tokens/workspace (login.ts:168). The previous design leaked the nonce only through `open()`'s argv, which is world-readable only on Linux `/proc//cmdline`; an HTTP endpoint on loopback is readable by every process on every OS (macOS and Windows both hide other users' argv), so for macOS/Windows this is a new exposure rather than a mitigated one. `docs/design/rest-api.md:379` concedes the race but asserts it "breaks the login visibly" — the only visible artifact is a 410 page in the browser, after which the CLI still prints a successful `Logged in as `.

verdict.reason: Every claimed element verified in-tree. login.ts:266-281 serves an unauthenticated 302 whose Location (built at login.ts:204-213) carries the 32-byte cliState nonce to whichever local client reaches /start first; the port is printed to stderr at login.ts:67 and is enumerable on loopback. The only control is the single-use startConsumed flag (login.ts:272-277), which prevents repeat but not first theft. With the nonce, an attacker drives GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim>&cliState=<stolen>: github-auth.guard.ts:67-77 / normalizeCliState (25-41) only pattern-checks the nonce and does not bind it to the minting flow, and auth.controller.ts:126-135 mints a code for the attacker's user and redirects it plus the echoed nonce to the victim's loopback listener. That callback passes stateMatches at login.ts:322, settles at login.ts:367-370, is exchanged at login.ts:86-90, and saveSession at login.ts:158-169 persists the attacker's tokens/workspaces while printing a success message — session fixation on the victim's CLI. docs/design/rest-api.md:379 concedes the race and claims it 'breaks the login visibly', but the traced code shows the CLI still completes and writes session.json, so no guard makes this unreachable. Authentication/nonce-exposure and auth-binding bypass are squarely in the security lane; the feature's own comments (login.ts:39-65) adopt the local-process threat model, so it is not out of scope.

finding.summary: The `--allow-unbound-callback` downgrade lever the comment claims to remove is still attacker-reachable: an attacker-sent nonce-less callback rewrites the timeout message into the "re-run with --allow-unbound-callback" nudge
finding.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set by *any* caller of `GET /callback?code=x` with no `state` (login.ts:306-315) — reachable by every local process and every page the browser visits — and it is the sole selector for the timeout error text (login.ts:378-380), which is `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` = "...re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback` to accept an unbound callback" (login.ts:222-226). Attack: a local process (1) consumes `/start` so the genuine browser leg can never produce a callback (login.ts:272-275 → 410), (2) sends one nonce-less `/callback?code=…`, (3) waits 30 s. The user is told, in the CLI's own voice, that the server is too old and to re-run with the flag; on that re-run `options.allowUnbound` is true, so the very next nonce-less callback the attacker sends is accepted outright (login.ts:306 short-circuits, 328-370 settles) and the attacker's code becomes the victim's session. The in-code rationale ("letting one of those abort the login … would hand an attacker a downgrade lever", login.ts:298-305) and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 assert this lever is gone; it is only delayed by the 30-second timeout. Deciding the message from an attacker-settable flag is the defect — the skew signal should come from something the attacker cannot set (e.g. the absence of the echo on a callback whose nonce matched, or a server capability probe).

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. `sawUnboundCallback` (login.ts:248) is set by any unauthenticated nonce-less `GET /callback?code=…` (login.ts:306-315) — reachable by any local process or visited page — and it is the sole selector for the timeout error text (login.ts:373-383), which is UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE instructing the user to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback` (login.ts:222-226). The genuine browser leg can be suppressed by racing the single-use `/start` (login.ts:266-281, second hit → 410 at 272-275), guaranteeing the 30s timeout fires with the attacker-chosen message; the port is discoverable from stderr (login.ts:67) and `open()` argv (login.ts:72). On the nudged re-run, `allowUnbound` is true so line 306 short-circuits, line 322's mismatch check is skipped (`received !== null` false), and the attacker's nonce-less code settles the login at 328-370 and is exchanged/saved as the session (login.ts:80-168). No guard restricts who can set the flag; the immediate warn at 311-314 is informational only. The in-code rationale (login.ts:298-305) and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 plus docs/design/cli.md:225-237 assert this downgrade nudge is NOT attacker-reachable, so it is not an accepted documented risk. In-lane (auth binding weakening leading to authorization-code injection), so not out-of-scope.

finding.summary: The loopback listener validates no `Host`/`Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` header, so a page the browser visits can consume the single-use nonce hand-off (login denial), and a DNS-rebound origin reaches a secret-serving endpoint
finding.evidence:
The request handler only inspects `req.url` (login.ts:262) and never looks at `req.headers`. Consequences: (1) any page the victim's browser visits can `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:

/start', {mode:'no-cors'})` or embed an iframe across the ephemeral port range; the request is a simple GET so no preflight applies, `startConsumed` flips (login.ts:277) and the real browser leg gets the 410 — a remote-page denial of every `wafflebase login`, plus a nudge into the retry loop that finding #2 weaponises. (2) Because no `Host` allow-list is enforced, the endpoint is reachable under an attacker-controlled hostname via DNS rebinding, i.e. from a same-origin JS context, which is precisely the configuration in which the same-origin argument in docs/design/cli.md:214-217 no longer holds; I could not construct a concrete browser primitive that reads a 302 `Location` even same-origin (`redirect:'manual'` yields an opaqueredirect), which is why confidence is low, but a loopback endpoint whose whole purpose is to serve a secret should not be answerable to requests whose `Host` is not `127.0.0.1:` or that carry a cross-site `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site`. Also unrestricted by method: a HEAD or POST to `/start` consumes it too.

verdict.reason: The absence is factually verified: the loopback handler in packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:261-371 branches only on url.pathname/searchParams (262) and never touches req.headers or req.method; a repo-wide grep for req.headers|rawHeaders|getHeader( scoped to packages/cli returns no matches, and login.ts:261 is the only Node HTTP server on the CLI path (no proxy/middleware in front — the raw handles are resolved at 397-408). Binding 127.0.0.1 at line 391 does not defeat DNS rebinding. Consequently any page the victim visits can burn the single-use /start with a plain GET (no preflight), flipping startConsumed at 277 so the genuine browser leg receives the 410 at 273 — a remotely triggerable denial of every `wafflebase login`, and the endpoint answers requests carrying an arbitrary Host or cross-site Origin. I found a Host/Origin check elsewhere in the repo (packages/design-editor/src/plugin/bridge.ts:109-111) but it is a different server and does not protect this path, so it is not a counterexample. Confidence is low, not because the missing check is in doubt, but because the nonce-disclosure leg is largely blocked by browser semantics the design doc already reasons about (docs/design/cli.md:214-217; a 302 Location is unreadable via no-cors/opaqueredirect, and the redirect target is cross-origin even under rebinding), leaving the demonstrable impact as remote login denial plus an unhardened secret-serving loopback endpoint.
